messages.content: What is the freezing point of water at a pressure of 10 kPa?

function.name: thermodynamics_calculate_boiling_point
function.description: Calculate the boiling point of a given substance at a specific pressure, provided in kilopascals (kPa) or atmospheres (atm). Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

substance.description: The chemical name of the substance for which to calculate the boiling point, such as 'water' or 'ethanol'.

pressure.description: The pressure at which to calculate the boiling point, expressed in the unit specified by the 'unit' parameter. This is a float type value.

unit.description: The unit of measurement for the pressure value. Accepts either 'kPa' or 'atm'.

message.content:
**Freezing (melting) point of pure water at ≈ 10 kPa**

| Condition | Approximate freezing point |
|-----------|----------------------------|
| **Pressure:** 10 kPa (≈ 0.099 bar) | **–6 °C** |

---

### How that figure comes out

Water’s solid‑liquid coexistence line (the “ice I” melting curve) rises with increasing pressure because ice is *less* dense than liquid water.  
A convenient way to estimate how much the melting temperature shifts when you move away from the normal‐atmospheric reference (1 atm = 101.3 kPa) is to use the empirical slope of the melting curve:

\[
\frac{dT_{\text{melt}}}{dP}\;\approx\;+\,0.07 \,\text{°C / bar}
      \quad(\text{or }+0.0007 \,\text{°C / kPa})
\]

Starting from the known melting point at 1 atm (0 °C):

```
ΔP   = 10 kPa – 101.3 kPa = –91.3 kPa
ΔT   = (−91.3 kPa) × (+0.0007 °C/kPa)
     ≃ −0.064 °C per kPa × 91.3 kPa
     ≃ –6.4 °C
```

So the expected freezing point drops from 0 °C down to roughly **–6 °C** at 10 kPa.

> **Note**  
> • The calculation assumes the usual hexagonal ice Ih structure and ignores minor effects due to impurities or isotopic composition.  
> • If the pressure falls below the triple point (~0.006 atm or 0.61 kPa), ice no longer melts; instead it sublimes directly into vapour.

If you need more precise values—for example, if your application involves high‑accuracy cryogenic processes—consult detailed experimental data tables or perform an integration of the Clausius–Clapeyron relation using measured latent heats and volumes.
